content:
A staff manual is where you write down how paid work runs. When the first administrator or ministry director joins the payroll, unclear hours, private files, and unofficial posts create fights you could have avoided.

This reference covers work duties and official communications. It does not write your church's beliefs, a personal-conduct code, or a discipline ladder. Have a qualified attorney review the manual before anyone is asked to follow it. Everyfield does not certify the manual. Evry will not interpret it or decide a conduct case.

---

## Keep the manual on assigned work

Write the manual for employees whose work you direct. Name the job, who the person reports to, and how questions about the schedule or pay get answered. Follow your bylaws for who may adopt the manual. A note from the Senior Pastor is not the manual until the body your bylaws name has approved it.

Do not use this manual to restate Launch Team expectations. The leadership overview asks ministry leaders to share the church's vision. That is a different document from employment rules. If you also use volunteers, do not assume employee rules fit them. Say who the manual covers.

| Topic | Where it belongs |
| --- | --- |
| Duties, hours, and reporting | This manual |
| Official church accounts | This manual |
| Personal posts that share private facts or speak as the church | This manual |
| Beliefs the church has already approved | A separate document. Do not invent the list here. |
| Calling, character, or fitness | People named in your bylaws, not software |

<Callout type="tip">
If you want belief or public-conduct expectations beyond assigned work, put them in a separate document. Point to the statement your church has already approved. Do not draft beliefs in the staff manual. Have your attorney review that separate document before you use it in hiring or discipline.
</Callout>

---

## Give people a reporting route

Name the supervisor for each role. Say how a staff member raises a question about hours, pay, or a workplace concern. Name a second person to receive a report when the concern is about the supervisor.

The EEOC encourages employers to prevent unlawful harassment by telling employees that unwelcome harassing conduct will not be tolerated, and by establishing a complaint or grievance process. Its harassment page, checked October 26, 2026, lists coverage of 15 or more employees under Title VII and the ADA, and 20 or more under the ADEA. A smaller church may still want a written route. Those thresholds do not, by themselves, tell you whether a law covers your church.

Describe the route in plain words. Ask counsel which retaliation rules apply before you promise a specific protection. Do not promise a particular outcome, and do not ask Evry to judge the complaint.

<Callout type="important">
EEOC harassment guidance checked October 26, 2026. That page says it is being reviewed and will be revised. Confirm current coverage and complaint guidance with the EEOC, and have a qualified attorney apply it to your church, before you rely on a headcount threshold.
</Callout>

---

## Protect private information

Name what staff may not share outside the people who need it for their work. Include personnel files, donor records, counseling conversations, and information about minors. The HR records article covers retention and restricted access. Point staff to that practice. Do not invent a shorter discard date in the manual.

A public reply is the wrong place for those facts. The reviews article treats an official reply as a church statement and keeps private matters out of comments. Use the same line here. If a comment needs a private follow-up, send the person to the church office. Do not ask them to post sensitive details.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"He who goes about as a slanderer reveals secrets, But he who is faithful in spirit conceals a matter."* — Proverbs 11:13 (LSB)
</Callout>

---

## Assign official accounts

Official accounts speak for the church. Name an owner for each account, and name who else may post, reply, or send messages. Give each person a separate login. Remove that access when the job ends.

Google's Business Profile help says additional owners and managers can edit info, respond to reviews, and manage posts. It also says each user needs a separate Google Account so you do not share a password. Owners can add and remove users. Check the current role names on every platform you use before you write them into the manual. Role names differ by platform.

A post or reply from an official account is a church statement, even when a staff member typed it. Read it that way before it goes out. Do not use a personal profile to look like the church's official reply.

<Callout type="warning">
Do not share the password for a church account. A shared login hides who posted, and you cannot shut it off cleanly when someone leaves. Remove the person's access instead.
</Callout>

---

## Draw a narrow line for personal posts

Personal accounts are not church accounts. The manual should still cover two work problems. Staff may not post private church information. Staff may not present a personal post as an official church statement. Ask them to speak in their own name when they are not using an account you assigned.

Do not build the manual around reading personal accounts. Washington law is one example, not a national rule. RCW 49.44.200 says an employer may not request, require, or coerce an employee or applicant to disclose login information for a personal social networking account. That section still allows an employer to require login information for an account provided because of the job, or for a device the employer supplies. Ask the state agency that enforces employment law whether your state has a similar limit before you request any login.

Do not copy another church's social media rules. Those rules may assume a belief covenant or a labor setting you have not adopted. This article leaves broader alignment expectations unstated on purpose. If your church wants them, write them in a separate document that cites the statement the church has already approved.

---

## Have an attorney read it before adoption

Employment coverage is not one rule. Title VII's religious-employer provision, 42 U.S.C. section 2000e-1, says the subchapter shall not apply to a religious corporation, association, educational institution, or society with respect to the employment of individuals of a particular religion to perform work connected with carrying on its activities. Read that limit as written. Ask counsel whether it applies to a role, and which federal, state, and local rules still apply to pay, safety, confidentiality, and account control. The statute page used here is the 2023 edition. Confirm the current text.

The NLRB's jurisdictional standards page says the Board will not assert jurisdiction over employees of a religious organization who are involved in effectuating the religious purpose of the organization, such as teachers in church-operated schools. The same page says the Board has asserted jurisdiction over employees in operations of a religious organization that did not have a religious character, such as a health care institution. Do not assume a secular handbook's labor language fits your staff, and do not assume it never could. Your attorney makes that call.

Point the manual to practices you already document elsewhere. Payroll classification, clergy tax treatment, and hiring forms belong in the payroll article. Record retention belongs in the HR records article. A manual that contradicts those articles will confuse the person who has to follow both.

Do not paste an at-will clause from another handbook. Ask counsel what, if anything, to say about how employment ends, and whether the manual should say it is not a contract. Do not promise job security the church has not approved.

Ask each employee to acknowledge the current manual. Keep that acknowledgment with the personnel file. When you change a rule, date the change, have counsel review it, and give staff the new version. An old unsigned draft on a shared drive is not the policy.

---

## Check the draft before you hand it out

- [ ] The manual names who it covers and who each person reports to.
- [ ] It says how to record time and who approves extra hours, where those rules apply to the job.
- [ ] It gives a route for harassment or another workplace concern, including a route that does not stop with the person accused.
- [ ] It names private information staff may not share, and it points to your restricted personnel files.
- [ ] It names an owner for each official account, forbids shared passwords, and says access ends when the job ends.
- [ ] Personal-post rules stay limited to private church information and claims to speak for the church.
- [ ] It does not ask for personal social-media logins. You checked your state's rule.
- [ ] A qualified attorney has reviewed the manual against the laws that apply to your church.
- [ ] Each employee acknowledges the current version, and that record stays with the personnel file.
excerpt: Document work duties, reporting lines, private information, and control of official church accounts. Keep personal-post rules narrow.
title: Staff Policy Manual and Official Communications

sources.claim: The EEOC encourages employers to prevent unlawful harassment by communicating that it will not be tolerated and by establishing a complaint process.
sources.quote: They should clearly communicate to employees that unwelcome harassing conduct will not be tolerated. They can do this by establishing an effective complaint or grievance process

sources.claim: EEOC harassment-page coverage figures are 15 employees for Title VII and the ADA, and 20 for the ADEA, and the page itself is under revision.
sources.quote: The information on this webpage is being reviewed for compliance with the law and executive orders and will be revised.

sources.claim: The same EEOC page states numerical coverage thresholds for Title VII, the ADA, and the ADEA.
sources.quote: 15 or more employees under Title VII and the ADA, 20 or more employees under the ADEA

sources.claim: Title VII's religious-employer provision is limited to employment of individuals of a particular religion for the organization's work.
sources.quote: to a religious corporation, association, educational institution, or society with respect to the employment of individuals of a particular religion to perform work connected with the carrying on by such corporation, association, educational institution, or society of its activities.

sources.claim: The NLRB says it will not assert jurisdiction over some religious-purpose employees, and that it has asserted jurisdiction over some nonreligious operations of religious organizations.
sources.quote: The Board will not assert jurisdiction over employees of a religious organization who are involved in effectuating the religious purpose of the organization, such as teachers in church-operated schools. The Board has asserted jurisdiction over employees who work in the operations of a religious organization that did not have a religious character, such as a health care institution.

sources.claim: Washington bars an employer from coercing disclosure of a personal social-networking login. It is an example, not a national rule.
sources.quote: Request, require, or otherwise coerce an employee or applicant to disclose login information for the employee's or applicant's personal social networking account

sources.claim: Washington's personal-account limit does not forbid requiring login information for an employment-provided account or an employer-supplied device.
sources.quote: An account or service provided by virtue of the employee's employment relationship with the employer; or (ii) an electronic communications device or online account paid for or supplied by the employer

sources.claim: Google Business Profile owners and managers can edit the profile, respond to reviews, and manage posts, and each user should have a separate Google Account rather than a shared password.
sources.quote: Additional owners and managers can help you handle daily operations. They can edit info, respond to reviews, and manage posts.

sources.claim: Google tells profile owners to give each user a separate Google Account instead of sharing a password.
sources.quote: To access and manage Business Profiles without the need to share your password, each user needs their own Google Account.

sources.claim: A Google Business Profile owner can add and remove users and has full control of the profile.
sources.quote: As the owner, you have full control over the profile. You can add or remove users, manage profile info, and even delete the profile.

rulings: Bryan ruled B8 = Option A: "Work duties and official communications" (2026-10-26 1:31 PM ET).

Wording call: title is Staff Policy Manual and Official Communications, and the slug is administrative/legal/staff-policy-manual-and-official-communications, rather than the backlog title. Option A covers work duties and official communications, not a personal-conduct social media policy.
Wording call: phase 0 and sort_order 6, placed after HR Records and Required Forms in administrative/legal, because the manual is adopted when staff are hired, not as a launch-week task.
Wording call: who adopts the manual follows the church's bylaws. The article does not assign that vote to the Senior Pastor or to elders.

Wording call: belief and public-conduct expectations are mentioned only as a separate document that must cite the church's already approved statement. This draft does not supply beliefs, discipline steps, or exceptions.
Wording call: Washington RCW 49.44.200 is an example of a state personal-account rule, in the same way other legal articles use one state's statute. It is not stated as national law.
